draft.title: Language that conveys experience
card: An inner experience, such as anxiety or joy, is hard to state directly. Writers use the way they write to let the reader feel it.
Diction
the exact words chosen. A writer who says a character "clutched" a cup instead of "held" it shows tension through one verb.
Imagery
language that builds a picture or a sense, often through a comparison. "Worry was a swarm of wasps in her chest" lets us feel the worry as sharp and hard to escape.
Rhythm
the beat of the sentences. Short, broken sentences can feel tense or rushed. Long, flowing ones can feel calm or joyful.
draft.remember: Precise words, images and rhythm let a reader feel an experience, not just be told about it.

a.q: Which sentence uses imagery to convey a character's anxiety?
opts: His thoughts were a tangle of knotted wire
He felt very anxious about the test
He sat at his desk and waited for the bell
He was worried, and he said so to Dad
a.why: The comparison to knotted wire builds a picture that lets us feel his mind as tight and stuck. The other options state or describe the feeling plainly, without a picture.
a.clue: Look for the option that compares the feeling to something we can picture.

b.q: Leila runs onto the field. The writer uses short, clipped sentences: "Whistle. Breath. Go. Her legs shook." What does the rhythm mainly suggest?
opts: Nervous tension and a rush of adrenaline
Calm, relaxed confidence before the game
Boredom as the match drags on
A slow, thoughtful memory of the past
b.why: Short, broken sentences make the pace quick and tense, which matches shaking legs and a held breath. Calm confidence would more likely suit long, flowing sentences, so it is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Think about what short, broken sentences do to the pace.

a.best: His thoughts were a tangle of knotted wire

b.best: Nervous tension and a rush of adrenaline

a.q: A writer changes "She walked to the stage" to "She edged towards the stage". What does this change in diction convey?
opts: Her reluctance or fear about reaching the stage
Her eagerness to begin the performance
Her pride in how far she has come
Her calm focus on the task ahead
a.why: To edge is to move slowly and cautiously, so the new verb shows she is holding back out of fear or reluctance. Eagerness is tempting because she is still moving towards the stage, but an eager person would hurry, not edge.
a.clue: Picture how someone moves when they edge forward.
